pub.methodologyTitle: How AgriPrice measures prices and makes forecasts
pub.methodologyDescription: Where our prices come from, how we clean and aggregate them, and when we publish (or withhold) a forecast.
pub.m_sourcesBody: Prices come from the sources below. Each observation keeps its source, market, date and original currency and unit.
pub.m_clean1: Every observation is converted to a price per kilogram, using conversion factors specific to the crop and country, and to US dollars using that day's exchange rate. The original amount and unit are kept.
pub.m_clean2: Each new price is compared with the last 90 days of prices for the same crop in the same region (or the whole country when the region has too few). We use a robust z-score: the median and the median absolute deviation, on a log scale, so a few extreme values can't move the reference.
pub.m_clean3: Unusual prices that no other report corroborates are held for review by our data team instead of being published. Sources we trust less go to review more often.
pub.m_agg: Published prices are daily and weekly averages of approved observations per market. Pages show when each price was last reported, and nothing is shown where no price was reported.
pub.m_fc1: Forecasts use a gradient-boosted model that predicts a likely range (the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles) for 1, 3 and 6 months ahead, from past prices, seasons, nearby markets, weather, exchange rates and fuel prices.
pub.m_fc2: Every model is tested on past data it didn't see (rolling-origin backtests) and is only used if it beats a seasonal baseline.
pub.m_guardTitle: When we don't publish a forecast
pub.m_guard: No forecast is better than a misleading one. A forecast is withheld when a series has fewer than {weeks} weeks of history, when its latest price is more than {days} days old, or when the backtest error (MAPE) for that horizon is above {mape}%.
pub.m_explainTitle: Why a forecast says what it says
pub.m_explain: Each forecast lists the factors that pushed it up or down (SHAP values), so you can see whether a rise comes from the lean season, the weather or the exchange rate.
pub.aboutDescription: AgriPrice publishes crop prices and price forecasts so farmers, traders and buyers can decide when and where to sell.
pub.about1: AgriPrice collects crop prices from markets across {country}, checks them, and publishes them free of charge alongside forecasts of where prices are heading.
pub.about2: Farmers use it to choose when and where to sell, traders to compare markets, and researchers and policy makers to follow food prices.
pub.about3: We explain how every number is produced on our methodology page and show where each price comes from.
